argument: Building on de Beauvoir's analysis of revenge, this episode uses Nietzsche's genealogical method to show that guilt is not a natural response calibrated to victims but an inherited, self-directed form of self-punishment that once served social control. In a post-God world, people still inherit Judeo-Christian guilt and its demand for self-denial, but without a divine authority to give that punishment meaning, leaving many in self-hatred. Nietzsche points to art as a model of meaning that doesn't depend on staking a claim to objective truth, offering an alternative to the ascetic ideal's binary of true and false.
keyIdeas: De Beauvoir argues that because we can never control another person's subjectivity, revenge can't force a wrongdoer to feel the victim's pain; instead it functions as a symbolic statement that governs future behavior through punishment.

Nietzsche applies a Darwin-style genealogy to guilt: moral intuitions weren't written into human nature but were inherited and propagated within specific social environments, much like physical traits.

Before Judeo-Christian morality, virtues tracked social class (courage for warriors, strength for kings); the oppressed class invented the category of 'evil' to name the virtues of their oppressors, creating the good/evil binary known as slave morality.

Nietzsche is skeptical of fixed moral categories like good and evil, illustrated by the sand dune image: reality is an unstable, constantly shifting process that no fixed category can fully capture, so even compassion can sometimes do more harm than good.

In a 'God is dead' world, people still inherit the sense that certain desires must be renounced and punished, but without God to give that punishment legitimate meaning, leaving them in self-hatred; art offers a model of meaning that doesn't require staking a claim to truth.

terms.def: Nietzsche's method of tracing the historical and social origin of a moral feeling rather than assuming it is simply natural.
The value system of the historically oppressed class (self-sacrifice, humility, altruism) that came to define 'goodness' after the concept of evil was created.
The pathological pattern of self-denial and binary thinking (good/evil, true/false) inherited from religious tradition.
Severe self-discipline and avoidance of indulgence; a systematized form of self-denial.
